title: Central and Southeast Asia face an infrastructure expansion choice between carbon-intensive lock-in and better-planned, climate-resilient, inclusive delivery
source_unit: OECD, Accelerating Sustainable Infrastructure Investments: Assessing Policies for Planning, Delivery and Financing in Central and Southeast Asia
geography: Indonesia, Kazakhstan, Mongolia, the Philippines, Thailand, and Uzbekistan; Central and Southeast Asia regional infrastructure systems

observations.period: 2026 report; infrastructure investment needs in six Central and Southeast Asian countries

denominator.unit: countries covered by the OECD Sustainable Infrastructure Programme in Asia analysis

annual_infrastructure_gap.unit: reported infrastructure investment gap across the covered regions

sustainability_alignment_cost.value: about 1 percent of GDP in most countries
sustainability_alignment_cost.unit: additional reported cost of aligning infrastructure with climate and sustainability objectives, relative to total investment needs

lock_in_risk.value: Without reform, current investment patterns could entrench carbon-intensive and climate-vulnerable systems; aligned policies could support more sustainable, resilient, and inclusive infrastructure

observations.method: OECD synthesis of the Sustainable Infrastructure Programme in Asia, implemented from 2021-2026, covering strategic planning, sectoral policies, financial systems, and regional analysis.
observations.uncertainty: The figures are regional estimates and policy-analysis results, not household-level costs or a forecast of realized investment; country definitions, sector coverage, and scenario assumptions matter for interpretation.
observations.subgroup: Residents and firms in the six countries, infrastructure users, governments, investors, workers, communities exposed to climate risks, and people affected by energy, transport, and industrial projects.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher sustainable-infrastructure spending can improve resilience and services while increasing public debt, land conflict, tariffs, construction disruption, or unequal access if governance and distributional safeguards are weak.

observations.period: 2026 report; energy and transport investment pipeline

denominator.unit: SIPA countries covered by the OECD infrastructure-pipeline assessment

coal_capacity.unit: gigawatts of new coal capacity reported as under development across the six countries, approximately

transport_pattern.value: Road-based transport dominates future investment plans

misalignment.value: Infrastructure pipelines continue to prioritize carbon-intensive assets, particularly in energy and transport

observations.method: OECD assessment of infrastructure pipelines and sectoral policies in the six countries.
observations.uncertainty: Pipeline status is not the same as final approval, construction, operation, or emissions outcome; the public summary does not provide project-level timelines, ownership, financing, or cancellation probabilities.
observations.subgroup: Energy and transport users, project developers, coal and infrastructure workers, urban and rural communities, governments, financiers, and people exposed to air pollution and climate risk.
observations.counterinterpretation: Coal and road investments may respond to real access, reliability, freight, mobility, and development needs; transition policy must address those service needs rather than treating infrastructure choices as only emissions decisions.

observations.period: 2026 report; planning, appraisal, and project-preparation capacity

implementation_gap.value: All six countries have national development and climate strategies, but commitments are not yet systematically translated into investment decisions

project_bottleneck.value: A shortage of well-prepared, bankable sustainable infrastructure projects is identified as a major bottleneck

integrated_appraisal.value: Integrated cost-benefit analysis can increase the benefit-cost ratio of sustainable projects by up to tenfold when overlooked environmental and social benefits are counted

observations.method: OECD review of planning frameworks, project preparation and evaluation practices, sectoral policies, and financial systems, including SIPA experience.
observations.uncertainty: The up-to-tenfold result is an analytical finding under specified appraisal conditions, not a guaranteed return for every project; benefit valuation, discounting, data quality, and distributional weights shape the result.
observations.subgroup: Planning ministries, local governments, project-preparation facilities, investors, communities affected by project appraisal, and public agencies responsible for budgets and delivery.
observations.counterinterpretation: More integrated appraisal can improve decisions but can also create technical barriers, obscure contested values in monetized analysis, or privilege projects that can demonstrate benefits in formal models.

observations.period: 2026 report; finance, resilience, nature, and institutional delivery

denominator.unit: countries covered by the OECD regional infrastructure assessment

climate_exposure.value: Floods, droughts, heatwaves, and sea-level rise are already affecting infrastructure systems across both regions

finance_constraints.value: Underdeveloped financial markets, limited non-bank participation, nascent risk-sharing instruments, and persistent fossil-fuel subsidies constrain sustainable-investment flows

governance_constraints.value: Limited technical capacity, fragmented governance, and weak coordination across ministries and levels of government hinder planning and implementation

nature_based_solutions.value: Nature-based solutions remain underutilized despite reported cost-effectiveness and environmental co-benefits

observations.method: OECD regional analysis of financial systems, climate resilience, nature-based solutions, institutional capacity, and governance across the six countries.
observations.uncertainty: The public summary identifies constraints and opportunities but does not quantify avoided losses, project-level resilience, finance mobilization, or who benefits from nature-based investments.
observations.subgroup: Climate-exposed households and communities, infrastructure users, public agencies, financial institutions, engineering and construction firms, and local governments.
observations.counterinterpretation: Institutional and finance reforms may unlock investment without guaranteeing affordability, local consent, maintenance, ecological integrity, or protection for communities with the least bargaining power.

boundary: This record adds a Central and Southeast Asian infrastructure-delivery signal on climate lock-in, investment gaps, coal and road pipelines, project preparation, appraisal, sustainable finance, resilience, nature-based solutions, and institutional coordination. It is an OECD policy assessment, not a household affordability study, a project-by-project audit, a causal evaluation of the tenfold appraisal result, or proof that recommendations will be implemented equitably.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official OECD publication page reviewed for country coverage, infrastructure-gap and alignment-cost estimates, coal and road pipeline findings, strategy-to-investment implementation gap, integrated appraisal result, climate exposure, financial constraints, nature-based solutions, and governance constraints.
